description: Comprehensive 50-Question Physics Question Bank for Wedge-Shaped Film Interference

questions.question: Why is the fringe at the line of contact between the two glass plates dark in reflected monochromatic light?
options: Reflection at the lower optically denser glass surface introduces a Stokes phase shift of π radians (λ/2 path difference)
The glass absorbs 100% of the light at zero film thickness
Refraction index of air drops to zero at the line of contact
Constructive interference cancels all odd harmonics
questions.answer: Reflection at the lower optically denser glass surface introduces a Stokes phase shift of π radians (λ/2 path difference)
questions.correct_option: Reflection at the lower optically denser glass surface introduces a Stokes phase shift of π radians (λ/2 path difference)
questions.explanation: At the contact edge t = 0. Reflection from the denser glass medium adds a phase jump of π rad (λ/2), causing destructive interference and producing a permanent dark fringe.

questions.question: Why are the interference fringes formed in a wedge-shaped film straight, parallel, and equidistant?
options: Loci of constant film thickness on optically flat planar plates are straight lines parallel to the contact apex
The travelling microscope lens produces straight virtual images regardless of plate curvature
Photons repel each other transversely in the air gap
Reflection angle is 45 degrees along the entire wedge
questions.answer: Loci of constant film thickness on optically flat planar plates are straight lines parallel to the contact apex
questions.correct_option: Loci of constant film thickness on optically flat planar plates are straight lines parallel to the contact apex
questions.explanation: Fringes of equal thickness (Fizeau fringes) follow contours of identical gap thickness t. For planar plates with constant wedge angle α, these contours form straight parallel lines.

questions.question: What is the formula to calculate spacer wire diameter d using fringe width β, wedge length L, and wavelength λ?
questions.explanation: Since fringe spacing β = (λ * L) / (2 * d), rearranging directly yields spacer diameter d = (λ * L) / (2 * β).

questions.question: What happens to the fringe width β if a thicker wire is used as the spacer?
options: Fringe width decreases and fringes crowd closer together because β is inversely proportional to wire diameter d
Fringe width increases and fringes become wider apart
Fringe width remains unchanged because it only depends on wavelength
Fringes turn into concentric circular Newton rings
questions.answer: Fringe width decreases and fringes crowd closer together because β is inversely proportional to wire diameter d
questions.correct_option: Fringe width decreases and fringes crowd closer together because β is inversely proportional to wire diameter d
questions.explanation: Because β = (λ * L) / (2 * d), increasing d steepens the wedge angle α = d / L, causing fringe spacing β to shrink.

questions.question: What is the condition for dark interference fringes (minima) in a thin air wedge observed in reflected light at near-normal incidence?
questions.explanation: Destructive interference occurs when total path difference Δ = 2t + λ/2 = (2m + 1)λ/2, which simplifies to 2t = mλ.

questions.question: If the air film (μ = 1) is replaced by a transparent liquid film of refractive index μ = 1.33, what happens to the fringe width β'?
options: Fringe width decreases to β' = β / μ
Fringe width increases to β' = β * μ
Fringe width is completely unaffected by medium refractive index
All fringes disappear due to total internal reflection
questions.answer: Fringe width decreases to β' = β / μ
questions.correct_option: Fringe width decreases to β' = β / μ
questions.explanation: The effective optical path within the film is 2μt, making fringe width β' = λ / (2μα) = β / μ.

questions.question: What is the small wedge angle α in radians for two plates of length L separated by a spacer wire of diameter d?
questions.answer: α ≈ d / L
questions.correct_option: α ≈ d / L
questions.explanation: Using the small angle trigonometric approximation, tan(α) ≈ α ≈ d / L in radians.

questions.question: Why must the travelling microscope carriage be moved in one continuous direction during measurement?
options: To eliminate mechanical backlash (lost motion) in the lead-screw and vernier nut assembly
To prevent optical polarization changes in the eyepiece reticle
Because the microscope can only focus when traveling forward
To ensure monochromatic light does not undergo Doppler shifts
questions.answer: To eliminate mechanical backlash (lost motion) in the lead-screw and vernier nut assembly
questions.correct_option: To eliminate mechanical backlash (lost motion) in the lead-screw and vernier nut assembly
questions.explanation: Reversing lead-screw motion introduces pitch play and deadband backlash error, spoiling precision micrometer vernier readings.

questions.question: What happens if a polychromatic white light source is used instead of monochromatic light?
options: A few colored fringes are visible near the zero-order dark contact apex, beyond which uniform white illumination appears
An infinite number of sharp black and white fringes are produced
Complete darkness results due to destructive interference of all colors
A continuous rainbow diffraction spectrum forms on the screen
questions.answer: A few colored fringes are visible near the zero-order dark contact apex, beyond which uniform white illumination appears
questions.correct_option: A few colored fringes are visible near the zero-order dark contact apex, beyond which uniform white illumination appears
questions.explanation: Because different wavelengths have different fringe spacings, only a few overlapping colored fringes appear near t = 0. At larger t, path difference exceeds the short coherence length of white light.

questions.question: In an experiment using Sodium yellow light (λ = 589.3 nm), wedge length L = 100.0 mm, and spacer diameter d = 40.0 μm, what is the theoretical fringe width β?
In a wedge-shaped thin film of angle θ and refractive index µ, what is the formula for the fringe width β of equidistant fringes?
questions.explanation: For normal incidence, path difference between consecutive fringes changes by λ, corresponding to an advance Δx = β such that 2µ(Δx * θ) = λ, giving β = λ / (2µθ).

questions.question: If an air wedge film (µ = 1) is formed by placing a spacer of thickness t at a distance L from the edge of contact, what is the fringe width β?
questions.explanation: Since the wedge angle is θ ≈ t / L, substituting into β = λ / (2θ) gives β = λL / (2t).

questions.question: How does the fringe width β change if the air film between the glass plates is replaced by a liquid of refractive index µ = 1.33?
options: The fringe width decreases by a factor of 1.33 (fringes become closer together)
The fringe width increases by a factor of 1.33
questions.answer: The fringe width decreases by a factor of 1.33 (fringes become closer together)
questions.correct_option: The fringe width decreases by a factor of 1.33 (fringes become closer together)
questions.explanation: Since β = λ / (2µθ), introducing a medium with µ > 1 reduces the optical wavelength to λ/µ, compressing the fringe width: β_liquid = β_air / µ.

questions.question: What is the condition for destructive interference (dark fringes) in a wedge-shaped film under normally incident light?
questions.explanation: Due to reflection at the lower optically denser boundary, an abrupt phase shift of π (equivalent to λ/2 path shift) occurs. Total path difference Δ = 2µt_x + λ/2 = (2n+1)λ/2, which simplifies to 2µt_x = nλ.

questions.question: What is the condition for constructive interference (bright fringes) in a wedge-shaped film of refractive index µ under normal illumination?
questions.explanation: Setting total path difference 2µt_x + λ/2 = nλ gives 2µt_x = (2n - 1)λ/2 for maximum brightness.

questions.question: Why is the line of contact (apex of the wedge where thickness t = 0) dark in reflected light?
options: At t = 0, the path difference is purely the λ/2 phase shift from reflection at the denser medium, causing complete destructive interference
Light cannot enter the apex because the gap is zero
Both light rays are completely absorbed by glass
Total internal reflection traps all light inside the top plate
questions.answer: At t = 0, the path difference is purely the λ/2 phase shift from reflection at the denser medium, causing complete destructive interference
questions.correct_option: At t = 0, the path difference is purely the λ/2 phase shift from reflection at the denser medium, causing complete destructive interference
questions.explanation: At the contact line t = 0, optical path difference is Δ = 0 + λ/2 = λ/2 (phase difference π), producing total destructive interference (dark fringe).

questions.question: If the wedge film is viewed in transmitted light rather than reflected light, what is the appearance of the line of contact (t = 0)?
options: Bright, because no relative phase shift occurs between the two transmitted rays
Dark, exactly the same as reflected light
questions.answer: Bright, because no relative phase shift occurs between the two transmitted rays
questions.correct_option: Bright, because no relative phase shift occurs between the two transmitted rays
questions.explanation: In transmission, interfering rays undergo two internal reflections or none; there is no net π phase shift, so path difference at t = 0 is zero (constructive interference = bright).

questions.question: What geometric shape do the interference fringes have in an ideal flat-surfaced wedge-shaped film?
options: Straight, parallel lines running parallel to the line of contact
questions.answer: Straight, parallel lines running parallel to the line of contact
questions.correct_option: Straight, parallel lines running parallel to the line of contact
questions.explanation: Each locus of constant film thickness t_x is a straight line parallel to the apex of the wedge; hence the fringes of equal thickness are straight and parallel.

questions.question: If Sodium light (λ = 589.3 nm) illuminates an air wedge where L = 10 cm and spacer thickness t = 0.05 mm, what is the fringe width β?
How is a wedge-shaped film setup used to determine the thickness t of a very thin sheet of paper or wire?
options: By counting the number of fringes over a known length L and applying t = (N * λ * L) / (2 * x) or t = λL / (2β)
By weighing the wire on a microbalance
By measuring electrical resistance of the glass plates
By measuring refraction angle with a spectrometer
questions.answer: By counting the number of fringes over a known length L and applying t = (N * λ * L) / (2 * x) or t = λL / (2β)
questions.correct_option: By counting the number of fringes over a known length L and applying t = (N * λ * L) / (2 * x) or t = λL / (2β)
questions.explanation: Knowing the distance L from apex to spacer and measuring fringe spacing β with a travelling microscope allows direct calculation: t = λL / (2β).

questions.question: What happens to the fringe width β if the spacer is pushed further away from the edge of contact (increasing L)?
options: Fringe width β increases (fringes spread farther apart)
questions.answer: Fringe width β increases (fringes spread farther apart)
questions.correct_option: Fringe width β increases (fringes spread farther apart)
questions.explanation: Since β = λL / (2t), increasing L while keeping spacer thickness t constant decreases the wedge angle θ = t/L, which widens the fringe spacing β.

questions.question: What happens to the fringes if a thicker wire is inserted as the spacer at the same distance L?
options: The wedge angle increases, causing fringes to crowd closer together (β decreases)
The central fringe shifts to white
questions.answer: The wedge angle increases, causing fringes to crowd closer together (β decreases)
questions.correct_option: The wedge angle increases, causing fringes to crowd closer together (β decreases)
questions.explanation: A thicker wire increases wedge angle θ = t/L. Since β = λ / (2θ), the fringes pack more densely together.

questions.question: What type of light source must be used to observe clear, high-contrast, multi-order interference fringes in a wedge film?
options: Monochromatic extended light source (such as Sodium vapor lamp with a diffusing glass plate)
A multi-colored incandescent bulb without filter
A fluorescent tube directly above the plate
questions.answer: Monochromatic extended light source (such as Sodium vapor lamp with a diffusing glass plate)
questions.correct_option: Monochromatic extended light source (such as Sodium vapor lamp with a diffusing glass plate)
questions.explanation: An extended monochromatic source provides rays over a range of angles that illuminate a wide viewing area with single wavelength coherence.

questions.question: Why is a glass plate inclined at 45° to the vertical placed above the wedge film in a travelling microscope setup?
options: To reflect light from the horizontal source down onto the film at normal incidence, while letting reflected light pass upward to the microscope
To focus the light into a point
To polarize the light at Brewster's angle
questions.answer: To reflect light from the horizontal source down onto the film at normal incidence, while letting reflected light pass upward to the microscope
questions.correct_option: To reflect light from the horizontal source down onto the film at normal incidence, while letting reflected light pass upward to the microscope
questions.explanation: A 45° semi-transparent beam distributor directs illumination vertically downward onto the film at 90° normal incidence and transmits the returning pattern up into the microscope objective.

questions.question: What happens to the interference fringes if white light is used instead of monochromatic sodium light?
options: Only a few colored fringes are seen near the edge of contact, followed by uniform white illumination
An infinite series of sharp black-and-white lines appears
The entire film turns completely black
questions.answer: Only a few colored fringes are seen near the edge of contact, followed by uniform white illumination
questions.correct_option: Only a few colored fringes are seen near the edge of contact, followed by uniform white illumination
questions.explanation: Because each wavelength has a different fringe width β(λ), overlapping colored fringes blur into uniform white light beyond the first few orders.

questions.question: In optical workshop metrology, how are wedge fringes used to test the optical flatness of a polished glass surface?
options: If the test surface is perfectly flat, fringes are perfectly straight and parallel; curvature in fringes reveals surface imperfections
By measuring how much light is absorbed by the surface
By heating the plate until fringes move
questions.answer: If the test surface is perfectly flat, fringes are perfectly straight and parallel; curvature in fringes reveals surface imperfections
questions.correct_option: If the test surface is perfectly flat, fringes are perfectly straight and parallel; curvature in fringes reveals surface imperfections
questions.explanation: Fringes act as optical contour elevation maps: a deviation of one fringe width corresponds to a surface height error of exactly λ/2 (≈ 0.3 µm).

questions.question: If the interference fringes observed in an air wedge curve towards the apex of the wedge, what does this indicate about the glass surface?
options: The surface has a convex contour error (bulges outward)
The surface has a concave depression
The glass is absorbing sodium light
questions.answer: The surface has a convex contour error (bulges outward)
questions.correct_option: The surface has a convex contour error (bulges outward)
questions.explanation: Fringes follow lines of equal thickness. Curving towards the thin apex means the thickness increases earlier due to a convex elevation.

questions.question: If an optical flat test reveals fringes that bend towards the thicker side of the wedge, what surface defect is present?
options: A concave hollow or depression in the surface
A scratch parallel to the edge
questions.answer: A concave hollow or depression in the surface
questions.correct_option: A concave hollow or depression in the surface
questions.explanation: Bending toward the thicker edge indicates that the required thickness for that fringe occurs farther out, signifying a concave depression.

questions.question: Over a distance of 1.2 cm along an air wedge, exactly 20 bright fringes are counted using a sodium lamp (λ = 589 nm). What is the fringe width β?
questions.explanation: β = total distance / number of fringes = 1.2 cm / 20 = 0.06 cm = 0.60 mm.

questions.question: Using the measured fringe width β = 0.60 mm, λ = 589 nm, and plate length L = 10 cm, what is the calculated thickness of the spacer wire?
What optical classification applies to wedge film fringes and Newton's rings?
questions.answer: Fringes of equal thickness (Fizeau fringes)
questions.correct_option: Fringes of equal thickness (Fizeau fringes)
questions.explanation: Fringes produced by a thin film with variable thickness under near-normal illumination are localized Fizeau fringes of equal thickness.

questions.question: Where are the interference fringes localized in a wedge-shaped film?
options: Inside or very close to the upper surface of the film itself
questions.answer: Inside or very close to the upper surface of the film itself
questions.correct_option: Inside or very close to the upper surface of the film itself
questions.explanation: Fringes of equal thickness are localized within the film; the microscope objective must be focused directly on the film surface to view them sharply.

questions.question: Why do thick glass plates (e.g. 5 mm thick window glass) not show visible interference fringes under room light?
options: The path difference (2µt) far exceeds the coherence length of ambient light, causing fringe overlap into white light
Thick glass does not reflect any light
Thick plates bend light rays backwards
questions.answer: The path difference (2µt) far exceeds the coherence length of ambient light, causing fringe overlap into white light
questions.correct_option: The path difference (2µt) far exceeds the coherence length of ambient light, causing fringe overlap into white light
questions.explanation: Interference requires path differences within the temporal coherence length of the source. For thick plates (2µt >> λ), countless orders overlap, washing out the pattern.

questions.question: If an air wedge is subjected to uniform heating such that the spacer expands by Δt while L remains constant, how does the fringe width β change?
options: β decreases because wedge angle θ increases
questions.answer: β decreases because wedge angle θ increases
questions.correct_option: β decreases because wedge angle θ increases
questions.explanation: As the spacer expands (t increases), wedge angle θ = t/L increases. Since β = λ / (2θ), the fringe width decreases.

questions.question: What is the phase difference between the two interfering beams at the m-th dark fringe in a reflected wedge film?
questions.answer: (2m + 1) * π radians
questions.correct_option: (2m + 1) * π radians
questions.explanation: Destructive interference occurs when the total phase difference is an odd multiple of π: δ = (2m + 1)π radians.

questions.question: What is the phase difference between the two interfering beams at the m-th bright fringe in a reflected wedge film?
questions.answer: 2m * π radians (even multiple of π)
questions.correct_option: 2m * π radians (even multiple of π)
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when the total phase difference between the two waves is an even multiple of π (0, 2π, 4π, ...).

questions.question: If the angle of incidence i of light onto a wedge film is increased from 0° (normal) to an angle i > 0, what is the effective path difference?
questions.answer: Δ = 2 * µ * t * cos(r) + λ/2
questions.correct_option: Δ = 2 * µ * t * cos(r) + λ/2
questions.explanation: For oblique incidence at refraction angle r, the geometric path difference is 2µt cos(r), plus λ/2 from boundary reflection.

questions.question: How does increasing the angle of incidence from 0° to an oblique angle affect the fringe width in a wedge film?
options: Fringe width increases because cos(r) < 1 reduces the effective path difference rate
questions.answer: Fringe width increases because cos(r) < 1 reduces the effective path difference rate
questions.correct_option: Fringe width increases because cos(r) < 1 reduces the effective path difference rate
questions.explanation: Since β = λ / (2µθ cos r) and cos(r) < 1, the fringes spread slightly farther apart as incidence angle increases.

questions.question: If a drop of water (µ = 1.33) is placed at the edge of an air wedge, capillary action draws it in. How do the fringes behave?
options: The fringes immediately compress closer together (fringe width decreases by 1/1.33 ≈ 0.75)
The contact line becomes bright in reflection
questions.answer: The fringes immediately compress closer together (fringe width decreases by 1/1.33 ≈ 0.75)
questions.correct_option: The fringes immediately compress closer together (fringe width decreases by 1/1.33 ≈ 0.75)
questions.explanation: In water, β_water = λ / (2 * 1.33 * θ) = 0.752 * β_air. Fringes become noticeably denser.

questions.question: What happens to the apex contact fringe if the two glass plates are pressed tightly together with a clamp?
options: The central dark fringe broadens over the entire contact area where t = 0
The contact fringe turns into a bright spot
questions.answer: The central dark fringe broadens over the entire contact area where t = 0
questions.correct_option: The central dark fringe broadens over the entire contact area where t = 0
questions.explanation: Optical contact over a finite area maintains t = 0 everywhere within that zone, expanding the dark zero-order region across the contact contact patch.

questions.question: Can a wedge-shaped film be formed using a soap film held vertically in a wire frame?
options: Yes, gravity pulls liquid downward, creating a vertical thickness gradient that forms horizontal wedge fringes
No, soap films are always of constant thickness
No, soap films cannot reflect light
questions.answer: Yes, gravity pulls liquid downward, creating a vertical thickness gradient that forms horizontal wedge fringes
questions.correct_option: Yes, gravity pulls liquid downward, creating a vertical thickness gradient that forms horizontal wedge fringes
questions.explanation: Gravity drains liquid downward while surface tension holds the top, creating a vertical wedge with horizontal interference bands.

questions.question: In a vertical soap film, what does the appearance of a black band at the top indicate just before the film pops?
options: The film thickness at the top has become much less than λ/4 (approaching zero thickness)
The film has absorbed all incident light
The soap solution has turned into oil
The refractive index has become infinite
questions.answer: The film thickness at the top has become much less than λ/4 (approaching zero thickness)
questions.correct_option: The film thickness at the top has become much less than λ/4 (approaching zero thickness)
questions.explanation: When film thickness t << λ/4, path difference is dominated by the π phase shift, making the film appear completely black just before rupture.

questions.question: What is the ratio of fringe widths β1 / β2 for two air wedges of equal length L using spacers of thickness t1 = 20 µm and t2 = 60 µm?
questions.explanation: Since β ∝ 1/t, β1 / β2 = t2 / t1 = 60 µm / 20 µm = 3.

questions.question: If light of wavelength λ1 = 400 nm produces 30 fringes in a given wedge distance, how many fringes will λ2 = 600 nm produce over the same distance?
questions.answer: 20 fringes
questions.correct_option: 20 fringes
questions.explanation: Total distance = N * β. Since β ∝ λ, N1 * λ1 = N2 * λ2. Thus N2 = N1 * (λ1 / λ2) = 30 * (400 / 600) = 20 fringes.

questions.question: Why must the glass plates used to form an experimental air wedge have optically flat surfaces?
options: Any microscopic surface irregularities distort the straight fringes into irregular wavy lines
Refractive index varies across non-flat glass
questions.answer: Any microscopic surface irregularities distort the straight fringes into irregular wavy lines
questions.correct_option: Any microscopic surface irregularities distort the straight fringes into irregular wavy lines
questions.explanation: Fringes map optical film thickness; only optically flat plates guarantee that thickness increases linearly, producing straight, evenly-spaced fringes.

questions.question: In an experiment, if 50 fringes occupy a length of 2.5 cm, what is the wedge angle θ in radians (using λ = 500 nm)?
questions.answer: 0.0005 radians (0.5 mrad)
questions.correct_option: 0.0005 radians (0.5 mrad)

questions.question: What causes the contrast (visibility) of wedge film fringes to degrade when using a light source with a broad spectral bandwidth Δλ?
options: Fringes for different wavelengths gradually shift out of phase as order n increases, washing out the pattern
Broadband light travels slower through glass
The wedge angle changes with wavelength
questions.answer: Fringes for different wavelengths gradually shift out of phase as order n increases, washing out the pattern
questions.correct_option: Fringes for different wavelengths gradually shift out of phase as order n increases, washing out the pattern
questions.explanation: Fringe visibility V = (I_max - I_min) / (I_max + I_min) decays as path difference approaches the coherence length L_c ≈ λ² / Δλ.

questions.question: How can one experimentally distinguish between bright fringes of consecutive order (n and n+1)?
options: Order n+1 corresponds to an increase in film thickness of exactly Δt = λ / (2µ)
Order n+1 has twice the light intensity
Order n+1 has a different color in monochromatic light
questions.answer: Order n+1 corresponds to an increase in film thickness of exactly Δt = λ / (2µ)
questions.correct_option: Order n+1 corresponds to an increase in film thickness of exactly Δt = λ / (2µ)
questions.explanation: Moving from one bright fringe to the next corresponds to an increase in film thickness of exactly Δt = λ / (2µ).

questions.question: If an air wedge film has a small wedge angle of 1 minute of arc (1' = 2.909 x 10⁻⁴ rad), what is the fringe width for λ = 589 nm?
Why does an air wedge film not show interference fringes if the top plate is lifted to create an air gap of several centimeters?
options: The thickness exceeds the temporal coherence length of the light source, so wave packets no longer overlap in time
Light stops reflecting at larger distances
The glass plates lose mutual capacitance
questions.answer: The thickness exceeds the temporal coherence length of the light source, so wave packets no longer overlap in time
questions.correct_option: The thickness exceeds the temporal coherence length of the light source, so wave packets no longer overlap in time
questions.explanation: For path differences 2µt larger than the source coherence length, the two wave trains cannot maintain a fixed phase relationship, eliminating observable interference.
